title: Excel and Google Sheets for Small Business
subtitle: Build a working sales tracker, inventory sheet and monthly profit report in Excel or Google Sheets, on your phone or computer.
description: A practical spreadsheet course for women running small businesses. You will learn to enter clean records, use formulas such as SUM, IF, SUMIF, COUNTIF and XLOOKUP, and turn your figures into charts and a profit report you can trust and share.
outcomes: Set up and format a clean business spreadsheet in Excel or Google Sheets on a phone or computer
Use SUM, AVERAGE, IF, SUMIF, COUNTIF and absolute references correctly
Run a sales and expense tracker with a running balance and error checks
Keep an inventory sheet with lookups, reorder alerts and stock value
Produce charts and a one-page monthly profit report with gross and net margins
Share and protect business files safely
audience: Women who run or are starting a small business and can use a smartphone, and want to move their records from paper or memory into a spreadsheet.
tools: A smartphone (Android or iPhone) or a computer
Google Sheets (free with a Google account) or Microsoft Excel (free phone app with a Microsoft account, or desktop Excel)
Your real sales, expense and stock records, or realistic practice figures
Internet access to set up and back up (offline work is possible after setup)

modules.title: Spreadsheet foundations on phone and computer
modules.overview: Set up Excel or Google Sheets, learn the parts of a spreadsheet and enter clean, well-formatted records. Finish by writing your first formulas and protecting your file from loss and scams.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets for your business: Excel or Google Sheets, phone or computer
objectives: Name the parts of a spreadsheet: workbook, sheet, row, column, cell and range
Choose between Excel and Google Sheets for your phone or computer
Create, name and save your first business sheet
Type a simple multiplication formula that works out a sale amount

blocks.text: Many small businesses keep records in an exercise book, on scraps of paper or in their heads. That works until you need an answer quickly: how much did I sell last month, which product makes the most money, who still owes me? A **spreadsheet** is a grid on your phone or computer that stores your records and does the calculations for you. Change one number and every total that depends on it updates by itself.

The two spreadsheet programs you will meet most are **Microsoft Excel** and **Google Sheets**. They look and work in very similar ways, and almost every formula in this course is typed the same way in both. You can follow the whole course on either one, on a phone or on a computer.

blocks.name: spreadsheets
blocks.alt: A woman working with rows and columns of figures on a large screen
blocks.caption: A spreadsheet turns scattered sales and expense notes into one grid you can add up in seconds.

blocks.text: The parts of a spreadsheet

head: Word
What it means
Example
rows: The whole file you save and open
One page inside the file, shown as tabs at the bottom
A vertical line of cells, named by a letter
A horizontal line of cells, named by a number
One box where a column and row meet, named column letter then row number
A block of cells, written first cell, colon, last cell
C2:C10 means C2 down to C10
The strip at the top (marked fx) that shows what is really inside the selected cell

blocks.text: Which program, and on which device?

items: **Google Sheets** is free with a Google account (the same account as Gmail or your Android phone). It works in a web browser on a computer and in the Google Sheets app on Android and iPhone. Your work saves automatically to Google Drive. To work without data, open the app, find the file and switch on **Make available offline**.
**Excel for the web** is free with a Microsoft account at office.com and needs internet.

**The Excel mobile app** for Android and iPhone lets you create and edit files on a phone once you sign in with a free Microsoft account. Some advanced features need a paid Microsoft 365 subscription.

**Excel on a computer** (Windows or Mac) is the full version. It usually comes with a paid Microsoft 365 subscription or a one-time purchase. Files saved to OneDrive save automatically when AutoSave is on.

blocks.title: Excel or Google Sheets?
items: Microsoft Excel
Google Sheets
blocks.caption: Both do everything in this course; pick the one you can open most easily every day.
left: Full version on computer is paid
right: Works in browser and phone app
Easy to share with a partner

blocks.title: Phone users
blocks.text: Turn your phone sideways (landscape) to see more columns. Pinch with two fingers to zoom in on the cell you are typing in. If you have a cheap Bluetooth or OTG keyboard, typing formulas becomes much faster.
Your first business sheet

items: Open Google Sheets or Excel and create a new blank file (in Sheets tap the + button; in Excel choose Blank workbook).
Give the file a clear name, for example your business name and the year. In Sheets tap the title at the top; in Excel use File, then Save As.
Rename the first tab to Sales. On a computer double-click the tab; on a phone tap the tab and choose Rename.
In row 1 type the headings: A1 Date, B1 Item, C1 Quantity, D1 Unit price (₦), E1 Amount (₦).
Type one sale in row 2. In E2 type =C2*D2 and press Enter. The star * means multiply.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's first three sales
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu and wants to stop adding up sales on a calculator at night. Prices here are illustrative and approximate.
steps: Row 2: Date 05/10/2026, Item Noodles carton, Quantity 2, Unit price 9500. In E2 she types =C2*D2.
Row 3: Item Groundnut oil 1 litre, Quantity 3, Unit price 3200. In E3 she types =C3*D3.
Row 4: Item Bar soap, Quantity 6, Unit price 700. In E4 she types =C4*D4.
In E5 she types =E2+E3+E4 to get the day's total.
blocks.result: E2 shows 19000, E3 shows 9600, E4 shows 4200 and E5 shows 32800. If she later corrects the soap price to 750, E4 changes to 4500 and E5 to 33100 without her doing anything else.

blocks.text: That last point is the whole reason spreadsheets save time. You type the raw facts once (quantity and price), and the formulas do the arithmetic again every time a fact changes. You never retype a total.

blocks.title: What you type versus what you see
blocks.text: When a cell holds a formula, the cell shows the answer (19000) but the formula bar shows the formula (=C2*D2). If you are ever unsure whether a number was typed or calculated, tap the cell and look at the formula bar.

takeaways: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells named by column letter and row number, such as C5.
Excel and Google Sheets work almost the same; formulas in this course work in both.
Google Sheets and the Excel phone app are free to start with; save files online so you do not lose them.
Type raw facts once and let formulas such as =C2*D2 do the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Entering and formatting business data the right way
objectives: Lay out records as one row per transaction and one column per detail
Recognise text, numbers and dates and avoid entries that break calculations
Apply naira, thousands-separator and date formats
Freeze the heading row and adjust column widths

blocks.text: A spreadsheet can only calculate what it understands. If you type **N5,000** or **5k**, it sees words, not a number, and your totals will quietly be wrong. This lesson teaches the habits that keep data clean, then how to make it readable with formatting.

blocks.name: data-input
blocks.alt: A person typing entries into a form on a screen
blocks.caption: Clean entry habits at the typing stage save hours of fixing later.

blocks.text: The layout rules

items: **One row = one transaction.** Each sale, purchase or payment gets its own row.
**One column = one kind of detail.** Date in one column, item in another, amount in another. Never mix two details in one cell, such as 3 bags @ 2000.
**Headings in row 1 only**, short and clear, with the unit in brackets: Amount (₦), Weight (kg).
**No blank rows or columns** inside your records. Sorting, filtering and charts treat a blank row as the end of the data.
**Same spelling every time.** Transport and Transpot are two different categories to a spreadsheet. Later you will add drop-down lists to stop this.

blocks.text: Avoid merged cells and big decorative titles above your headings. A title such as MY SALES 2026 in row 1 with headings in row 3 confuses sorting, filtering, tables and charts. Put the title in the file name or the tab name instead, and keep row 1 for headings. If you want a heading to look wider, make the column wider rather than merging cells.

blocks.title: Clean data checklist
items: One row per transaction
One column per detail
Headings in row 1
No blank rows
Numbers typed as numbers
Consistent spelling
blocks.caption: Run through this list before you trust any total.

blocks.text: Text, numbers and dates
A quick check: by default, numbers line up on the **right** of the cell and text lines up on the **left**. If an amount sits on the left, the spreadsheet probably sees it as text and will not add it.

head: What you type
What the spreadsheet sees
Better entry
rows: Format the column as Plain text (Sheets) or Text (Excel) first, or type '08031234567
A date, read using your region setting
Quantity 3 in one column, unit price 2000 in the next

blocks.title: Day first or month first?
blocks.text: 05/10/2026 is 5 October in Nigeria but 10 May in the United States. In Google Sheets go to File, Settings and set Locale to Nigeria so dates read day first. Excel on a computer follows the region set in Windows or macOS. After setting it, type a date like 25/12/2026: if it lines up on the right, it was understood as a date.
Formatting that makes numbers readable

items: **Bold the headings.** Select row 1 and tap or click B. Add a fill colour so the heading row stands out.
**Thousands separators.** Select the amount column. In Excel: Home, Number group, the comma style button. In Sheets: Format, Number, Number. 125000 now shows as 125,000.

**Naira sign.** In Sheets: Format, Number, Custom currency, search Naira and pick ₦. In Excel and Sheets you can also use a custom number format: "₦"#,##0 (Excel: Format Cells, Number, Custom; Sheets: Format, Number, Custom number format). The value stays a number; only the display changes.
**Dates.** Select the date column and choose a date format such as 05/10/2026 or 5 Oct 2026.
**Column width.** On a computer, double-click the line between two column letters to fit the widest entry. On a phone, drag the edge of the column letter.

**Freeze the heading row.** Excel: View, Freeze Panes, Freeze Top Row. Sheets: View, Freeze, 1 row. On the Sheets app, tap the row number 1 and choose Freeze. Now the headings stay visible as you scroll down.

blocks.title: Format whole columns
blocks.text: Select a whole column by tapping its letter before you format it. New rows you add later will then pick up the naira or date format automatically.

blocks.title: Decimals and kobo
blocks.text: Formatting changes only what you see, not what is stored. If a cell holds 1333.33 and you set it to show no decimals, it displays 1,333 but still adds up as 1333.33. If you need the stored value itself rounded, use =ROUND(A2,0) for whole naira or =ROUND(A2,2) for kobo.

blocks.title: Worked example: tidying Amaka's fabric record
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sells ankara and lace in Onitsha. Her first sheet had entries like 'N18k', '2 yds @ 4500' and phone numbers missing the leading zero.
steps: She splits '2 yds @ 4500' into Quantity 2, Unit price 4500 and Amount =C2*D2, giving 9000.
She replaces 'N18k' with 18000 and applies the format "₦"#,##0, so it shows ₦18,000.
She formats the Phone column as Plain text and retypes 08031234567, which now keeps its zero.
She sets the Sheets locale to Nigeria, bolds row 1 and freezes it.
blocks.result: Every amount now sits on the right of its cell, the total at the bottom finally matches her calculator, and the headings stay on screen when she scrolls through 60 rows.

takeaways: One row per transaction, one column per detail, headings in row 1, no blank rows.
Type numbers without N, k or commas; let formatting add the naira sign and separators.
Numbers sit on the right, text on the left: use this to spot problems.
Set your region so dates read day first, and freeze the heading row.

lessons.title: Your first formulas: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX, and keeping your file safe
objectives: Write formulas with + - * / and brackets in the right order
Use SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT on a range
Copy a formula down a column on a computer and on a phone
Protect your business file with backups, version history and safe habits

blocks.text: Every formula starts with an **equals sign =**. Without it, the spreadsheet treats what you type as plain text. After the = you can use numbers, cell addresses and functions (ready-made calculations with names like SUM).

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person beside a large calculator doing sums
blocks.caption: Formulas do the calculator work for you and redo it every time a number changes.

blocks.text: Spreadsheets follow the same order as school maths (BODMAS): brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. So =2+3*4 gives **14**, but =(2+3)*4 gives **20**. When in doubt, add brackets.

blocks.title: Point, do not type numbers
blocks.text: Write =C2*D2, not =3*1200. If the quantity in C2 changes, the first formula updates; the second does not. On a computer you can click a cell while writing a formula to insert its address; on a phone, tap the cell.

blocks.title: Building a formula
items: Select answer cell
Type =
Tap first cell
Type operator
Tap next cell
Press Enter
blocks.caption: The same six moves build almost every simple formula on phone or computer.

blocks.text: Five functions you will use every week

head: Function
What it does
Example
rows: Adds every number in a range
Adds the numbers and divides by how many there are
Counts how many cells contain numbers

blocks.text: COUNT only counts cells holding numbers. Its partner **COUNTA** counts every cell that is not empty, text included, so =COUNTA(A2:A50) on a column of customer names tells you how many sales you recorded. If COUNT and COUNTA give different answers on an amount column, some amounts have been typed as text: a quick way to find hidden problems.

A shortcut for SUM: select the empty cell under a column of numbers and use **AutoSum** (the Σ button on Excel's Home tab; in Google Sheets, the Σ Functions button on the toolbar, then SUM). Always check the range it guesses before pressing Enter.

blocks.title: Worked example: a week of sales at Bisi's food stand
blocks.context: For example, Bisi sells rice and stew in Ibadan. She records daily takings in B2:B7 for Monday to Saturday: 12500, 8000, 15200, 9800, 21000 and 30500.
steps: Weekly total in B9: =SUM(B2:B7).
Average day in B10: =AVERAGE(B2:B7).
Worst day in B11: =MIN(B2:B7). Best day in B12: =MAX(B2:B7).
She is closed on Sunday. If she types 0 for Sunday in B8 and changes the ranges to B2:B8, AVERAGE now divides by 7.
blocks.result: Total ₦97,000; average day about ₦16,166.67 over six trading days; worst day ₦8,000 (Tuesday); best day ₦30,500 (Saturday). With a 0 for Sunday the average drops to about ₦13,857.14, because AVERAGE counts zeros but ignores empty cells. She leaves Sunday blank so her average reflects trading days only.

blocks.text: Copying a formula down a column

Put totals in the same place on every sheet, for example two rows under the last entry or in a separate summary area at the top. When you insert rows in the middle of a range, the SUM range grows automatically. Rows added after the last entry may not be included, so tap the total afterwards and check the range in the formula bar. Module 3 shows tables, which grow by themselves.

items: **On a computer:** select the cell with the formula, then drag the small square at its bottom-right corner (the fill handle) down. Double-clicking the square fills down as far as the data next to it goes.
**On a phone:** tap the formula cell, tap Copy, select the cells below (drag the blue handles), then tap Paste. This works in both apps.
Each copied formula adjusts its row automatically: =C2*D2 becomes =C3*D3 in the next row. Module 2 explains why, and when you must stop it.

blocks.text: Keeping your business file safe

items: **Save online.** Google Sheets saves to Google Drive as you type. In Excel, save the file to OneDrive and keep AutoSave on. A phone that is stolen or dropped in water should not take your records with it.
**Use version history.** Google Sheets: File, Version history. Excel with OneDrive: File, Info, Version History. You can go back to yesterday's copy if something is deleted.
**Download a backup** once a month (File, Download, Microsoft Excel .xlsx in Sheets; Save a Copy in Excel) and keep it somewhere else, such as email to yourself.
**Lock your phone** with a PIN or fingerprint. Your sheet may hold customer names, phone numbers and debts, which are personal data you must protect.

blocks.title: Spreadsheet scams
blocks.text: Do not open spreadsheet attachments from strangers, especially ones that ask you to 'Enable Content' or 'Enable Macros' to see an invoice or a payment alert. That is a common way of installing harmful software. Real bank alerts come by SMS or your banking app, not as spreadsheets.

takeaways: Every formula starts with =; brackets are worked out first.
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT answer most everyday questions about a column.
AVERAGE counts zeros but ignores empty cells, so decide which you mean.
Copy formulas down with the fill handle or copy and paste; they adjust row by row.
Save online, use version history and never enable macros in files from strangers.

steps: Add a Daily takings sheet with Day in column A and Amount in column B for the last six or seven trading days.
Calculate the total, average, smallest and largest day with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX.
Check the total once with a calculator.
Switch on offline access or AutoSave, then open version history to see that it works.

quiz.q: Halima types =C4*D4 into E4. What does the cell show?
options: The value in C4 multiplied by the value in D4
An error, because formulas need the word SUM
quiz.explain: A formula starting with = calculates. The cell shows the result; the formula bar shows =C4*D4.

quiz.q: A trader typed 'N7500' as an amount and her SUM total is too low. What is the best fix?
options: Retype it as 7500 and apply a naira number format
quiz.explain: N7500 is text, so SUM ignores it. Type the number only and let formatting show the naira sign.

quiz.q: What does =(1500+500)*3 return?
quiz.explain: Brackets first: 1500+500 = 2000, then 2000 multiplied by 3 = 6000.

quiz.q: Daily sales are in B2:B7, with one day typed as 0 and another left blank. Which statement about =AVERAGE(B2:B7) is true?
options: It ignores both the 0 and the blank
It counts both the 0 and the blank
It counts the 0 but ignores the blank
quiz.explain: AVERAGE includes zeros in the count but skips empty cells.

quiz.q: Kemi's phone numbers keep losing the first 0. What should she do?
options: Format the column as text (Plain text in Sheets) before typing, or start with an apostrophe
Type the numbers with spaces between digits only
quiz.explain: A number cannot start with 0, so the spreadsheet drops it. Treating the column as text keeps the 0.

quiz.q: Someone sends a spreadsheet 'payment confirmation' on WhatsApp and it asks you to Enable Macros to view it. What should you do?
options: Enable macros so you can see the payment
Do not enable it; check your bank app or SMS alert instead
Print it and then enable macros
quiz.explain: Requests to enable macros in unexpected files are a common way to spread harmful software. Confirm payments in your bank app.

modules.title: Guided practice: references, IF and a working tracker
modules.overview: Learn to copy formulas safely with absolute references, then build a complete sales and expense tracker using IF. Finish by learning to find and fix both loud and silent spreadsheet errors.

lessons.title: Relative and absolute references: copy formulas without breaking them
objectives: Explain why a copied formula changes its cell addresses
Lock a cell with the $ sign so it stays fixed when copied
Use one input cell for a rate such as commission or discount
Work out each item's share of a total with an absolute reference

blocks.text: In Module 1 you copied =C2*D2 down and it became =C3*D3, =C4*D4 and so on. That is a **relative reference**: the formula remembers the position of the cells relative to itself (two columns left, one column left), not their fixed addresses. Most of the time this is exactly what you want.

Sometimes, though, every row must use the **same** cell, for example one commission rate or one discount rate typed once at the top of the sheet. If you copy a normal formula, the address slides down with it and points at empty cells. The fix is an **absolute reference**, written with dollar signs: **$H$1**. The $ has nothing to do with money here; it means 'do not move'.

blocks.name: data-processing
blocks.alt: A person arranging blocks of data that feed into one result
blocks.caption: Locking one input cell lets the same rate feed every row of your sheet.

blocks.title: Relative versus absolute
items: Relative (H1)
Absolute ($H$1)
blocks.caption: Use relative for row-by-row data and absolute for one shared input cell.

blocks.text: How to add the dollar signs

items: **Type them** yourself: =E2*$H$1. This works everywhere, including on a phone.

**On a Windows computer**, click inside the cell address in the formula and press **F4**. Each press cycles H1, $H$1, H$1, $H1. On some laptops you press Fn+F4. In Excel for Mac the shortcut is Command+T.
In Google Sheets on a computer, F4 also cycles the dollar signs (Fn+F4 on many laptops).

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's sales commission
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells shoes in Lagos and pays her sales assistant 5% commission on every sale. She types the rate once in H1 as 5% and keeps sale amounts in column E, rows 2 to 5: 19000, 7500, 12000 and 4800.
steps: Wrong way: in F2 she types =E2*H1 and copies it down. F3 becomes =E3*H2, but H2 is empty, so F3, F4 and F5 all show 0.
Right way: in F2 she types =E2*$H$1 and copies it down. F3 becomes =E3*$H$1, still pointing at the rate.
She adds totals: E7 =SUM(E2:E5) and F7 =SUM(F2:F5).
In January she raises the rate to 6% by changing only H1.
blocks.result: Commissions are ₦950, ₦375, ₦600 and ₦240. Total sales are ₦43,300 and total commission ₦2,165, which is exactly 5% of ₦43,300. At 6% every row recalculates at once and the total becomes ₦2,598.

blocks.text: Mixed references in a price grid

Mixed references lock only the row or only the column. They are handy for a quick price grid. Suppose unit prices sit down column A (A2 is 1200, A3 is 2500) and quantities run across row 1 (B1 is 1, C1 is 5, D1 is 10). In B2 type =$A2*B$1 and copy it across and down the whole grid. The column A part stays locked to the price, and the row 1 part stays locked to the quantity. C2 shows 6000 (1200 x 5) and D3 shows 25000 (2500 x 10), all from one formula.

blocks.title: Name your input cell
blocks.text: Instead of $H$1 you can give the cell a name. Excel: select H1, type CommissionRate in the Name Box left of the formula bar and press Enter. Google Sheets: Data, Named ranges. Then =E2*CommissionRate works and reads like a sentence. Named cells behave like absolute references when copied.
Share of total: a very common use

Which item brings in most of your money? Divide each amount by the grand total. The grand total sits in one cell, so it must be absolute. In G2 type =E2/$E$7, copy it down to G5, then format column G as a percentage (Excel: Home, % button; Sheets: Format, Number, Percent).

The shares add up to 100%, which is a handy check. If you had written =E2/E7 and copied it down, the next row would divide by E8, an empty cell, and show a #DIV/0! error. You will learn to read errors like that in Lesson 2.3.

blocks.title: Keep inputs together and labelled
blocks.text: Put every rate or setting your formulas depend on in one small, clearly labelled area, such as H1 Commission rate, H2 Discount rate. Colour those cells light yellow so you and anyone helping you know they are inputs that can be changed. Formulas then point at them with $ signs.

blocks.title: Discounts work the same way
blocks.text: If you give a 10% discount on a price in D2 with the rate in H2, the discounted price is =D2*(1-$H$2). For a price of 2500 that gives 2250. The brackets matter: without them the formula would multiply first and give a wrong answer.

takeaways: Normal addresses like E2 are relative and slide when copied.
Dollar signs, as in $H$1, lock an address so every copy points at the same cell.
Type the $ yourself on a phone, or press F4 on a Windows computer.
Keep rates in one labelled input area and point to them with absolute references.
Share of total uses =amount/$total$ and the shares should add up to 100%.

lessons.title: Build a sales and expense tracker with IF
objectives: Lay out a single tracker for money in and money out
Write IF formulas with comparison signs such as =, > and <>
Split amounts into money in and money out and keep a running balance
Work out weekly totals and the difference between money in and money out

blocks.text: Now you will build the tool most small businesses need first: one sheet that records every sale and every expense and tells you, at any moment, how much came in, how much went out and what is left. The key new function is **IF**, which lets a formula make a simple decision.

blocks.name: budgeting
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing a budget sheet with coins beside her
blocks.caption: One tracker shows money in, money out and the balance after every entry.

blocks.text: How IF works

The pattern is **=IF(test, value if true, value if false)**. The test compares two things. If the comparison is true, the cell shows the second part; if not, it shows the third part. Text must be inside straight double quotes, numbers must not be.

head: Sign
Meaning
Example test
True when
rows: B2 says Sale (capital letters do not matter)

blocks.text: The tracker layout

head: Column
Heading
What goes in it
rows: For example Food sales, Foodstuff, Gas, Packaging, Transport

blocks.text: The balance formula is the only one that changes after the first row: each row takes the balance from the row above, adds what came in and subtracts what went out. Copy J3 down, not J2.

blocks.title: From entry to answer
items: Record the transaction
Mark Sale or Expense
IF splits in and out
Running balance updates
Weekly totals
blocks.caption: You type four facts per row; the formulas do everything after that.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's food stand, Monday to Thursday
blocks.context: For example, Bisi sells plates of jollof at an illustrative ₦1,500 each. She records four days of sales and costs. Prices are approximate examples, not market figures.
steps: Row 2 Sale: 25 plates x 1500 = 37500. Row 3 Expense: Foodstuff 1 x 55000 = 55000.
Row 4 Sale: 30 x 1500 = 45000. Row 5 Expense: Gas refill 1 x 9000 = 9000.
Row 6 Sale: 22 x 1500 = 33000. Row 7 Expense: Takeaway packs 2 x 3500 = 7000.
Row 8 Sale: 28 x 1500 = 42000. Row 9 Expense: Transport 1 x 2500 = 2500.
Totals: H11 =SUM(H2:H9), I11 =SUM(I2:I9), and in J11 =H11-I11.
blocks.result: Money in ₦157,500, money out ₦73,500, difference ₦84,000, which matches the last running balance. The negative balance after row 3 shows the day her big foodstuff purchase came before the sales that paid for it, a useful warning about cash flow.

blocks.title: Money left is not the same as profit
blocks.text: The ₦84,000 is cash in minus cash out for these four days. Some of the foodstuff Bisi bought may still be in her store for next week, and she has not counted rent or her own time. Lesson 4.2 shows how to turn tracker figures into a proper profit report.
More useful IF formulas

items: Flag big spending: =IF(I2>20000,"Check","OK") puts Check beside any expense above ₦20,000.
Spot unpaid sales: with Paid or Unpaid in column K, =IF(K2="Unpaid",G2,0) gives an amount owed column you can SUM.
Avoid zeros cluttering a column: =IF(B2="Sale",G2,"") shows a blank instead of 0. SUM still works because it ignores empty text.
Show a message on the total: =IF(J11<0,"Spending more than earning","In surplus").

blocks.title: Spelling must match exactly
blocks.text: IF(B2="Sale",...) only works if column B says Sale. 'Sales', 'Sale ' with a trailing space, or 'sell' will all go to 0. Lesson 3.1 shows how a drop-down list removes this problem.
Keeping the tracker going

Add each new transaction in the next empty row at the bottom, in date order, and copy the formulas from the row above (or let a table do it, Lesson 3.1). Many people start a fresh tab each month, named for example Oct 2026, by duplicating last month's tab and deleting the old entries but keeping the headings and formulas. Fill the tracker daily, even if it takes only five minutes: entries typed the same day are far more accurate than ones remembered at the weekend.

Record the payment method too if it helps you, for example a column for Cash, Transfer or POS. When you reconcile at the end of the day, the transfer total should match the credits in your Opay, Moniepoint or bank app, and the cash total should match the money in your drawer.

takeaways: IF follows the pattern =IF(test, value if true, value if false); text goes in quotes.
One tracker with a Type column can hold both sales and expenses.
Money in and money out columns use IF; the running balance adds in and subtracts out row by row.
Cash left over is not yet profit; stock still on hand and other costs matter.
Spelling in the Type column must match the IF test exactly.

activity.title: Build your tracker
steps: Create a new tab called Tracker with the ten headings from this lesson.
Enter at least eight real or realistic transactions, mixing sales and expenses.
Add the Amount, Money in, Money out and Balance formulas and copy them down.
Add totals and check that money in minus money out equals the last balance.
Add one extra IF column, such as a Check flag for large expenses.
activity.evidence: Your Tracker tab with at least eight rows, working formulas and matching totals.

lessons.title: Finding and fixing spreadsheet errors
objectives: Read the common error codes and say what causes each
Find numbers stored as text that make totals silently wrong
Use Show Formulas and IFERROR to check and tidy a sheet
Cross-check totals so mistakes are caught early

blocks.text: Every spreadsheet user makes mistakes. The difference between a beginner and a confident user is knowing how to find them. There are two kinds: **loud errors**, where a cell shows a code such as #DIV/0!, and **silent errors**, where the sheet shows a number that looks fine but is wrong. Silent errors are more dangerous, so you will learn to hunt for them.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking a list of data entries with a tick mark
blocks.caption: Checking your sheet regularly catches small mistakes before they become wrong decisions.

blocks.text: The loud errors

head: What you see
What it means
Common cause in a business sheet
Fix
rows: Column too narrow to show the number or date
A large amount or a long date
Dividing by zero or by an empty cell
Fill the cell, or use IFERROR
Maths on something that is not a number
The spreadsheet does not recognise a word in the formula
=SUMM(B2:B7), or text in IF without quotes
Correct the spelling or add quotes
The formula points to a cell that no longer exists
You deleted a row or column the formula used
A lookup could not find the value
XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP for a product code not in the list
Google Sheets cannot read the formula

blocks.text: Spreadsheets also warn you about a **circular reference**, when a formula includes its own cell, such as =SUM(B2:B10) typed into B10. Move the total outside the range it adds.

blocks.title: The error-fixing loop
items: Spot something odd
Read the code
Check the cells used
Correct the cause
Recheck the total
blocks.caption: Go round the loop until the sheet and your calculator agree.

blocks.text: The silent error: numbers stored as text

SUM adds numbers and quietly skips anything it sees as text. If one amount was typed as N5,000 or pasted from WhatsApp with a hidden space, it is left out and the total looks believable but is short. Signs to look for: the number sits on the left of the cell, Excel shows a small green triangle in the corner, or COUNT on the column gives a smaller answer than COUNTA.

blocks.title: Worked example: Chioma's total that was too low
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells hair products in Port Harcourt. Her five sales on Friday were 12000, 18000, 5000, 9000 and 22000, but her sheet's SUM said 61000 while her calculator said 66000.
steps: She types =COUNT(B2:B6) and gets 4, while =COUNTA(B2:B6) gives 5. One cell is text.
She scans the column: B4 shows N5,000 on the left side of the cell.
She retypes B4 as 5000 and applies her naira format.
In Excel she could also click the warning icon next to a green-triangle cell and choose Convert to Number.
blocks.result: COUNT now returns 5 and SUM returns ₦66,000, matching the calculator. Without the check she would have under-recorded Friday by ₦5,000.

blocks.text: Tools that help you check

items: **Show formulas.** Excel: Formulas tab, Show Formulas. Google Sheets: View, Show, Formulas. Both use the shortcut Ctrl+` (the key above Tab). Every cell shows its formula, so a hand-typed number among formulas stands out at once.
**Check one row by hand.** After copying a formula down, tap a cell halfway down and read it in the formula bar. Does =E14*F14 really point at row 14?
**Trace in Excel.** Formulas, Trace Precedents draws arrows to the cells a formula uses.

**Cross-check totals.** Money in minus money out should equal the last running balance. Category totals should add up to the grand total. If two routes to the same number disagree, something is wrong.

blocks.text: Excel's green triangle does not only mean text numbers. It also appears when a formula differs from the ones around it, for example one row that adds instead of multiplies. Click the warning icon to read what Excel noticed before you decide to ignore it.
IFERROR: tidy, but use with care

**=IFERROR(formula, what to show instead)** shows something friendlier when a formula fails. For example, average price per unit =IFERROR(G2/E2,"") shows a blank instead of #DIV/0! on rows where quantity is still empty. It is useful for expected gaps, but do not wrap every formula in IFERROR: it can hide a real mistake, such as a misspelt function, behind a blank cell.

blocks.title: Undo is your friend
blocks.text: If a total suddenly changes to #REF! after you delete something, press Ctrl+Z on a computer or tap the undo arrow on a phone straight away. If it is too late, open version history and restore an earlier copy.

blocks.title: Make a check cell
blocks.text: Add one cell that tests your sheet, for example =IF(H11-I11=J9,"Balanced","Check totals"). If anything breaks the link between your totals and the running balance, it changes to Check totals the moment it happens.

takeaways: Loud errors show codes; each code points to a specific cause.
Silent errors, such as numbers stored as text, give believable but wrong totals.
COUNT smaller than COUNTA on an amount column means some amounts are text.
Show Formulas, one-row checks and cross-checks catch most mistakes.
Use IFERROR for expected gaps only, not to hide real problems.

activity.title: Error hunt
steps: Turn on Show Formulas in your Tracker and look for any cell holding a typed number where a formula should be.
Compare COUNT and COUNTA on your Amount column and fix any text amounts.
Deliberately type N3000 in a copy of a row, see the #VALUE! error, then fix it.
Add a check cell that confirms money in minus money out equals the last balance.
Note down any error you found and how you fixed it.
activity.evidence: A short note listing the errors found and fixed, plus a screenshot of your check cell showing Balanced.

quiz.q: Tunde puts a 7% delivery charge rate in H1 and types =E2*H1 in F2, then copies it down. Rows 3 onwards show 0. Why?
options: The rate must be typed as 0.7
The copied formulas point to H2, H3 and so on, which are empty
Multiplication does not work with percentages
quiz.explain: H1 is relative, so it slides down when copied. =E2*$H$1 keeps every row pointing at the rate.

quiz.q: Total sales are in E10. Which formula in G2 can be copied down to show each sale's share of the total?
quiz.explain: The sale amount should move row by row, but the total must stay fixed, so only E10 gets dollar signs.

quiz.q: What does =IF(B5="Expense",G5,0) show if B5 says Sale and G5 is 4000?
quiz.explain: The test is false because B5 is not Expense, so IF returns the third part, 0.

quiz.q: A running balance has 20000 in J6. Row 7 has 5000 money in and 8000 money out. What should =J6+H7-I7 return?
Amina's profit margin cell =B7/B2 shows #DIV/0!. What is the most likely cause?
options: B2, the sales cell, is empty or zero
quiz.explain: #DIV/0! appears when dividing by zero or by an empty cell.

quiz.q: Her SUM looks reasonable, but COUNT on the amount column gives 18 while COUNTA gives 20. What should she do next?
options: Find the two amounts stored as text and retype them as numbers
quiz.explain: Two cells hold text, so SUM is skipping them. The total is silently too low until they are fixed.

modules.title: Quality data and clear evidence: sorting, summaries and charts
modules.overview: Keep your data clean with sorting, filtering, tables and drop-down lists. Then turn it into evidence with SUMIF and COUNTIF summaries and charts that show how your business is really doing.

lessons.title: Sort, filter, tables and drop-down lists
objectives: Sort records safely without mixing up rows
Filter a sheet to show only the rows you need and total them with SUBTOTAL
Turn a range into a table that grows and copies formulas by itself
Add drop-down lists so categories are always spelled the same

blocks.text: Once your tracker has a few weeks of entries, you will want to ask questions such as: what were my five biggest sales, and how much did I spend on transport? **Sorting** puts rows in order. **Filtering** hides the rows you do not need for a moment. **Tables** and **drop-down lists** keep the data tidy as it grows. Together they are the quality controls of a business spreadsheet.

blocks.name: filter
blocks.alt: A person narrowing a large set of items down through a funnel
blocks.caption: Filtering shows only the rows that answer today's question, without deleting anything.

blocks.text: Sorting without breaking your rows

items: Tap any single cell inside your data (do not select just one column).
Excel: Data, Sort. Tick My data has headers, choose the column (for example Amount) and the order (Largest to Smallest).

Google Sheets on a computer: select the whole data range including headings, then Data, Sort range, Advanced range sorting options, tick Data has header row, choose the column and Z to A for largest first.
Google Sheets app: tap the column letter, then the three-dot menu, and choose a sort option. Check that whole rows moved together.

blocks.title: Never sort one column alone
blocks.text: If you select only the Amount column and sort it, the amounts move but the dates and items beside them do not. Every row is now wrong. Excel warns you and offers Expand the selection: always accept it. If it happens, undo straight away.

blocks.title: Sort or filter?
items: Sort
Filter
blocks.caption: Sort changes the order of rows; filter hides rows temporarily without changing anything.

blocks.text: Filtering

items: **Excel:** click inside the data, then Data, Filter (shortcut Ctrl+Shift+L). Arrows appear on each heading.
**Google Sheets:** Data, Create a filter. On the app, select the heading row, tap the three dots and choose Create a filter.
Tap the arrow on a heading and untick the values you do not want, or use Filter by condition (Sheets) or Number Filters (Excel), for example Greater than 20000.
A funnel icon on the heading reminds you a filter is on. Clear it when you are done, or you may forget rows are hidden.

blocks.text: To total only the visible rows after filtering, use **=SUBTOTAL(9,G2:G200)**. The 9 tells SUBTOTAL to add up; it ignores rows hidden by the filter, unlike SUM, which adds everything. This works the same way in Excel and Google Sheets.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima's transport spending
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs a small catering business in Kano and has 40 rows in her October tracker. She suspects transport is eating her profit.
steps: She turns on the filter and, on the Category arrow, ticks only Transport. Four rows remain: 2500, 3000, 1500 and 4000.
In a cell above her headings she has =SUBTOTAL(9,G2:G41). It now shows the transport total.
She clears the Category filter and sorts the whole range by Amount, Largest to Smallest, to see her biggest sales at the top.
She clears the sort by re-sorting by Date, oldest first.
blocks.result: Transport for October comes to ₦11,000 over 4 trips. SUM on the same column would still show the full total for all 40 rows, which is why SUBTOTAL is the right tool when filtering.

blocks.text: Tables: ranges that look after themselves

items: **Excel:** click inside your data and press Ctrl+T (or Insert, Table), tick My table has headers. Rows get banded colours and filter arrows.

When you type a new row directly under an Excel table, it joins the table and the formulas in calculated columns fill in automatically. Charts and SUM formulas that use the table's columns grow with it.
Excel tables can show a Total Row (Table Design tab, tick Total Row) that already uses SUBTOTAL, so it respects filters.
Inside a table, Excel may write formulas with column names, such as =[@Qty]*[@[Unit price]]. This means 'Qty times Unit price on this row' and works just like =E2*F2.
**Google Sheets:** select the data and choose Format, Convert to table. You get headings with filter menus and column types.

blocks.text: Drop-down lists stop spelling mistakes

items: Select the whole Type column below the heading (for example B2:B500).
Excel: Data, Data Validation. Under Allow choose List, and in Source type Sale,Expense. Click OK.
Google Sheets: Insert, Dropdown (or Data, Data validation), then add the options Sale and Expense.
Do the same for Category with your own list, for example Food sales, Foodstuff, Gas, Packaging, Transport, Rent.
Now each cell shows a small arrow. Tap it and pick from the list instead of typing.

blocks.title: Keep long lists on their own tab
blocks.text: If your categories or products change often, type them on a tab called Lists and point the drop-down at that range (in Excel's Source box, select the cells; in Sheets, choose Dropdown from a range). Add a new category there and every drop-down sees it.
Drop-downs matter because your IF, SUMIF and COUNTIF formulas match text exactly. A list makes every entry identical, so those formulas never silently miss a row.

takeaways: Click inside the data and sort the whole range, never one column alone.
Filters hide rows temporarily; clear them when you are done.
SUBTOTAL(9, range) totals only visible rows after filtering.
Excel tables (Ctrl+T) and Sheets tables grow and keep formulas consistent.
Drop-down lists keep categories spelled the same, so formulas match.

activity.title: Tidy your tracker
steps: Add drop-down lists to the Type and Category columns of your Tracker.
Turn your Tracker into a table (Ctrl+T in Excel, Format, Convert to table in Sheets).
Sort by Amount, largest first, and note your three biggest sales. Then sort back by Date.
Filter to one expense category and total it with SUBTOTAL(9, ...).
Clear the filter and write down what you learned.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your filtered tracker showing the SUBTOTAL result, and a note of your three biggest sales.

lessons.title: SUMIF and COUNTIF: totals by category, customer and month
objectives: Total amounts that meet one condition with SUMIF
Count matching rows with COUNTIF and average them with AVERAGEIF
Use SUMIFS for more than one condition, including a date range for a month
Build a summary table that updates itself and handles customer data responsibly

blocks.text: Filtering answers one question at a time. **SUMIF** and **COUNTIF** answer the same questions permanently: a small summary table that always shows spending by category, sales by product or how many customers still owe you, and updates every time you add a row.

blocks.name: organizing-data
blocks.alt: A person sorting coloured blocks into labelled groups
blocks.caption: SUMIF groups your rows by category and adds each group for you.

blocks.text: The three functions

head: Function
Pattern
Reads as
rows: =SUMIF(range to check, condition, range to add)
Add the amounts where the category matches
Count the rows where the condition is true
=AVERAGEIF(range to check, condition, range to average)
Average the amounts where the category matches

blocks.title: How SUMIF thinks
items: Look down Category
Match the condition
Pick same-row Amount
Add matches together
blocks.caption: SUMIF checks one column and adds the matching rows from another.

blocks.text: Writing conditions

items: Exact text: "Transport". Capital letters do not matter.
A cell holding the text: J2. This is how a summary table works, one category per row.
Numbers with signs go inside quotes: ">10000", "<=500", "<>0".
Joining a sign to a cell: ">="&K1 means greater than or equal to whatever is in K1.
Wildcards: "*rice*" matches any text containing rice, such as Rice 50kg or Fried rice.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's expenses by category
blocks.context: For example, Bisi's October expenses sit in a tracker with Category in C2:C9 and Amount in G2:G9: Foodstuff 55000, Gas 9000, Packaging 7000, Transport 2500, Foodstuff 12000, Transport 1500, Packaging 3500, Transport 2000.
steps: She lists categories in J2:J5: Foodstuff, Gas, Packaging, Transport.
In K2 she types =SUMIF($C$2:$C$9,J2,$G$2:$G$9) and copies it down to K5. The $ signs keep the ranges fixed while J2 moves to J3, J4, J5.
In L2 she types =COUNTIF($C$2:$C$9,J2) and copies it down to count entries per category.
K6 =SUM(K2:K5) gives the total. For trips she adds =AVERAGEIF(C2:C9,"Transport",G2:G9).
For large purchases she adds =COUNTIF(G2:G9,">5000").
blocks.result: Foodstuff ₦67,000 (2 entries), Gas ₦9,000 (1), Packaging ₦10,500 (2), Transport ₦6,000 (3), total ₦92,500, which matches =SUM(G2:G9). Average transport trip ₦2,000. Four expenses were above ₦5,000.

blocks.title: Always cross-check
blocks.text: The category totals must add up to the overall total of the Amount column. If they do not, a category is misspelt or missing from your summary list. This is the same cross-check idea from Lesson 2.3.
SUMIFS: more than one condition

**SUMIFS** adds rows that meet several conditions at once. Note the order is different: the range to add comes **first**. =SUMIFS(sum range, range1, condition1, range2, condition2, ...). For example, money spent on Transport in October only, with dates in column A:
=SUMIFS(G:G, C:C, "Transport", A:A, ">="&DATE(2026,10,1), A:A, "<"&DATE(2026,11,1))

DATE(2026,10,1) builds the date 1 October 2026 whatever your region setting, which avoids day-month confusion. Using 'less than 1 November' instead of 'up to 31 October' works for every month without worrying about 30 or 31 days. COUNTIFS works the same way for counting.
Best sellers and loyal customers

The same functions work on products and customers. On a Products summary, list each product and use =SUMIF(Tracker!D:D,A2,Tracker!E:E) to add up the units sold of the product named in A2 (with product names in column D and quantities in column E of the tracker). Sort the summary by that column to see your best sellers at the top. On the customer side, if you add customer names in column L, =COUNTIF(Tracker!L:L,"Mama Joy") counts how many times one customer bought from you. Customers with high counts are your loyal base; they are the people to tell first about new stock.

blocks.title: Whole columns and circular references
blocks.text: Ranges such as G:G (the whole column) are fine in both Excel and Google Sheets and save you from editing ranges later. Just never put the SUMIF formula itself inside the column it is adding, or you create a circular reference. Keeping summaries on a separate tab avoids this completely.
Customers and debts

Add a Paid column K (with a Paid or Unpaid drop-down) and a Customer column L to your tracker. Then =SUMIF(K:K,"Unpaid",G:G) gives the total owed to you and =COUNTIF(K:K,"Unpaid") the number of unpaid sales. =SUMIFS(G:G,L:L,"Mama Joy",K:K,"Unpaid") shows what one customer owes. A debtors list like this is often worth more than any chart.

blocks.title: Customer details are personal data
blocks.text: Names, phone numbers and what people owe are personal information. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 expects businesses to collect only what they need and keep it secure. Share summary totals, not customer lists, in groups; restrict who can open the file; and never post a debtors list publicly to shame customers.

Put your summary table on its own tab called Summary. Point the formulas at whole columns of the tracker (such as Tracker!G:G) or at the table you made in Lesson 3.1, so new rows are always included without you editing anything.

takeaways: SUMIF adds amounts that match one condition; COUNTIF counts the matching rows.
Use $ signs on the ranges so a summary formula can be copied down a list of categories.
SUMIFS puts the sum range first and can combine category and date conditions.
DATE(year, month, day) with >= and < gives clean month totals.
Customer data is personal data: share totals, protect the file.

activity.title: Make a Summary tab
steps: Create a Summary tab with your expense categories listed in one column.
Use SUMIF with $ ranges to total each category, and COUNTIF to count entries.
Check that the category totals add up to the Amount column total.
Add a SUMIFS formula that totals sales for the current month using DATE.
If you sell on credit, add a total owed using SUMIF on an Unpaid column.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Summary tab with category totals that match the overall total.

lessons.title: Charts that show how your business is doing
objectives: Choose the right chart type for the question you are asking
Insert and edit a chart in Excel and Google Sheets
Read a trend and work out growth from a chart's data
Avoid charts that mislead

blocks.text: A table of numbers tells the truth, but a chart tells it at a glance. A good chart answers one question: are sales rising, which month was best, where does my money go? A bad chart decorates a page and confuses the reader. This lesson is about choosing and making good ones.

blocks.name: charts
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a set of colourful charts on a board
blocks.caption: A clear chart lets a partner or lender see your business trend in seconds.

blocks.text: Pick the chart for the question

head: Question
Best chart
Why
rows: How did sales change month by month?
The line shows the direction over time
Which product or month sold most?
Which of many products sold most, with long names?
Long labels fit on the side
What share of spending goes to each category?
Pie chart, only with up to about 5 slices
Two bars side by side per month

blocks.title: A good business chart
items: Answers one question
Title states the message
Units shown, such as ₦
Columns start at zero
Few colours, clear labels
blocks.caption: Run through this before you share a chart with anyone.

blocks.text: Making a chart

items: Arrange your data in two columns: labels on the left (months or categories) and numbers on the right, with headings.
Select both columns including the headings.
Excel: Insert, Recommended Charts, then choose one. Google Sheets: Insert, Chart; the Chart editor opens on the right. On the Sheets app, tap + then Chart.
Change the chart type if needed (Excel: Chart Design, Change Chart Type; Sheets: Chart editor, Setup, Chart type).
Edit the title so it states the message, for example Sales rose 50% from July to December, not just Chart 1.
Add data labels if there are only a few points (Excel: the + button beside the chart; Sheets: Customise, Series, Data labels).

blocks.title: Worked example: Funke's six months of sales
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs a provisions shop in Abeokuta. Her monthly sales from July to December are 210000, 185000, 240000, 262000, 230000 and 315000, in B2:B7 with months in A2:A7.
steps: She selects A1:B7 and inserts a line chart.
Total in B8: =SUM(B2:B7). Average in B9: =AVERAGE(B2:B7).
Growth from July to December in B10: =(B7-B2)/B2, formatted as a percentage.
She titles the chart Sales rose 50% from July to December and labels the vertical axis Sales (₦).
blocks.result: Six-month total ₦1,442,000, average about ₦240,333 a month, growth 50%. The line dips in August and November and peaks in December, so she filters her tracker for those months to see what was different.

blocks.text: A pie chart of spending

Using Bisi's category totals from Lesson 3.2 (Foodstuff 67,000, Gas 9,000, Packaging 10,500, Transport 6,000), a pie chart shows Foodstuff at about 72.4%, Packaging 11.4%, Gas 9.7% and Transport 6.5%. The message is clear at once: buying foodstuff well (prices, quantities, waste) is where her savings must come from. Packaging and transport matter much less.

blocks.title: Charts that mislead
blocks.text: A column chart whose axis starts at ₦180,000 instead of zero makes a small rise look huge. Pie charts with ten thin slices are unreadable, and 3D effects distort sizes. In Excel or Sheets, check the vertical axis minimum is 0 for column and bar charts (Format Axis in Excel; Customise, Vertical axis in Sheets).
Keeping charts up to date

items: If your data is an Excel table or you selected whole columns, new rows appear in the chart automatically.
Otherwise, right-click the chart and choose Select Data (Excel) or open the Chart editor and edit the Data range (Sheets) to include new rows.
Copy a chart into WhatsApp or a report: in Sheets use the three-dot menu on the chart, Download, PNG image; in Excel right-click, Copy, or Save as Picture on a computer.

blocks.text: Two charts are usually enough for a small business owner: a line chart of monthly sales (or sales and expenses) and a pie or bar chart of where the money goes. Look at them on the same day each month and ask: what changed, and why?

For a quick picture inside a single cell, try a **sparkline**: a tiny line chart beside the numbers. In Google Sheets type =SPARKLINE(B2:B7) in an empty cell. In Excel on a computer, select the cell and choose Insert, Sparklines, Line, then pick the data range. A row of sparklines beside each product's monthly sales shows at a glance which products are rising and which are falling, without filling the sheet with large charts.

blocks.title: Sales versus expenses
blocks.text: Put months in column A, sales in B and expenses in C. Select all three columns and choose a clustered column chart. Months where the expense bar is taller than the sales bar jump out immediately.

takeaways: Line charts show change over time; column and bar charts compare; pies show shares of a whole.
Give every chart a title that states its message and show the units.
Growth is (new minus old) divided by old, formatted as a percentage.
Start column axes at zero and keep pies to about five slices.
Base charts on tables or whole columns so they update themselves.

activity.title: Chart your business
steps: Put your monthly (or weekly) sales in two columns with headings.
Insert a line chart and give it a title that states what happened.
Make a pie or bar chart of your expense categories from your Summary tab.
Check the axis starts at zero and the units are shown.
Write two sentences on what the charts show and one action you will take.
activity.evidence: Downloaded images of both charts and your two-sentence interpretation.

quiz.q: Joy selects only the Amount column and sorts it from largest to smallest. What happens?
options: Amounts move but the dates and items beside them stay put, so rows are mixed up
quiz.explain: Sorting one column alone breaks the link between the cells in each row. Always sort the whole range.

quiz.q: After filtering to show only Transport rows, which formula totals just the visible amounts in G2:G100?
quiz.explain: SUBTOTAL with 9 adds only rows not hidden by the filter; SUM adds every row.

quiz.q: Categories are in C2:C50 and amounts in G2:G50. Which formula totals Packaging?
quiz.explain: SUMIF checks the category range, matches Packaging and adds from the amount range.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to add a drop-down list to the Category column?
options: So entries are spelled identically and SUMIF or IF formulas never miss rows
To stop anyone opening the file
quiz.explain: Formulas match text exactly; a list removes spelling variations.

quiz.q: Sales were 200000 in March and 250000 in June. What does =(B3-B2)/B2 show, formatted as a percentage, if B2 is March and B3 is June?
Which chart best shows how monthly sales changed over a year?
quiz.explain: Line charts show direction over time. Pies show shares of one whole and are not for trends.

modules.title: Portfolio build: inventory, profit report and your complete workbook
modules.overview: Build an inventory sheet that looks up prices and warns you when to reorder, then a monthly profit report you can share. Finish by assembling everything into one business workbook with a routine that keeps it reliable.

lessons.title: Build an inventory sheet with XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP
objectives: Lay out a product list with cost price, selling price and stock levels
Calculate closing stock, stock value and reorder alerts
Fetch a product's price automatically with XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP
Link units sold from your sales log with SUMIF

blocks.text: Stock is often the biggest amount of money a small trader has tied up. An inventory sheet tells you what you have, what it is worth and what to reorder before customers find empty shelves. It also feeds prices into your sales log, so you stop typing prices by hand.

blocks.name: data-table
blocks.alt: A person working on a table of rows and columns on a laptop
blocks.caption: A product table with codes, prices and stock levels is the heart of an inventory sheet.

blocks.text: The Products tab

head: Column
Heading
Formula or entry
rows: Short unique code, such as P01
Name with size, such as Vegetable oil 1L
Units at the start of the month
Units sold this month (typed, or SUMIF from sales)
The quantity at which you restock

blocks.title: Worked example: Funke's provisions shop
blocks.context: For example, Funke tracks four products. Prices are illustrative and approximate.
steps: P01 Detergent 900g: cost 2100, sell 2500, opening 24, in 12, sold 30. Closing =24+12-30 = 6; reorder level 8, so Status shows Reorder. Value 6 x 2100 = 12600.
P02 Spaghetti 500g: cost 950, sell 1200, opening 40, in 0, sold 22. Closing 18; reorder level 10, OK. Value 17100.
P03 Vegetable oil 1L: cost 2800, sell 3300, opening 15, in 10, sold 9. Closing 16; reorder level 6, OK. Value 44800.
P04 Toothpaste: cost 1150, sell 1400, opening 20, in 0, sold 15. Closing 5; reorder level 6, Reorder. Value 5750.
Total stock value in K6: =SUM(K2:K5).
blocks.result: Two products need reordering (detergent and toothpaste) and Funke's stock on hand is worth ₦80,250 at cost. She filters the Status column for Reorder to make her shopping list for the market.

blocks.text: Looking up a price automatically

On your sales log you can type just the product code and let the sheet fetch the price. That is what lookup functions do: find a value in one column and return the matching value from another column on the same row.

blocks.title: How a lookup works
items: Type the product code
Search the Code column
Find the matching row
Return the price
Multiply by quantity
blocks.caption: The lookup replaces flipping through a price list by hand.

blocks.text: XLOOKUP (newer, easier)

=XLOOKUP(what to find, where to look, what to return, [if not found]). On a Sales tab with the code in B2: **=XLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$A$100,Products!$D$2:$D$100,"Not found")**. If B2 is P03, it returns 3300. Then the amount is =C2*D2 as before: a quantity of 2 gives 6600.

XLOOKUP works in Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, Excel for the web and Google Sheets. It looks for an exact match by default, can return a column to the left or right, and the 'if not found' part replaces the #N/A error with your own message.
VLOOKUP (older, everywhere)

If your Excel is 2019 or older, use VLOOKUP. =VLOOKUP(what to find, table, column number, FALSE). For the same job: **=VLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$K$100,4,FALSE)**. The 4 means 'return the 4th column of the table', which is Selling price (A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, D is 4).

items: The code you search for must be in the **first column** of the table. VLOOKUP cannot look to the left.
Always finish with **FALSE** for an exact match. Leaving it out tells VLOOKUP to find an approximate match, which can quietly return the wrong product's price.
If you insert a new column inside the table, the column number may now point at the wrong column. XLOOKUP does not have this problem.
Lock the table with $ signs so it does not slide when you copy the formula down.

blocks.title: #N/A means not found
blocks.text: If a lookup shows #N/A, the code typed does not exist in your Products list, or has an extra space or a letter O instead of a zero. Check the code, or use a drop-down list of codes so only real ones can be chosen.
Linking sales to stock

Instead of counting sold units by hand, let the Products tab add them up from the Sales tab. If the Sales tab has codes in column B and quantities in column C, then in Products G2 type **=SUMIF(Sales!$B:$B,A2,Sales!$C:$C)** and copy it down. Every sale you record now reduces closing stock and can trigger a Reorder alert automatically.

blocks.title: Count your shelves too
blocks.text: A spreadsheet only knows what you tell it. Once a month, physically count your stock and compare with Closing stock. A gap can mean breakage, expired goods, unrecorded sales or theft. Record the difference in a separate Adjustment column so the history stays honest.

takeaways: Closing stock = opening stock + stock in - units sold.
IF against a reorder level turns the sheet into an automatic shopping list.
XLOOKUP fetches a price by code and is available in newer Excel and Google Sheets.
VLOOKUP needs the code in the first column and FALSE for an exact match.
SUMIF from the Sales tab keeps units sold up to date; count real stock monthly.

lessons.title: A simple monthly profit report you can share
objectives: Calculate cost of goods sold from stock values and purchases
Work out gross profit, net profit and margins
Lay out a one-page monthly report with a comparison to last month
Share the report as a PDF and protect the formulas

blocks.text: Your tracker tells you cash in and cash out. Your inventory tells you what stock you hold. A **profit report** joins them to answer the question every business owner, partner, cooperative or lender asks: did the business actually make money this month, and how much?

blocks.name: report
blocks.alt: A woman holding a printed report with charts
blocks.caption: A one-page monthly report turns your sheet into evidence others can trust.

blocks.text: Key words, explained once

head: Term
Meaning
Formula
rows: Money earned from selling goods in the month
SUMIFS of sales for the month
What the goods you actually sold cost you
Opening stock value + purchases - closing stock value
What is left from sales after paying for the goods
Gross profit as a share of sales
Running costs: rent, transport, data, electricity or fuel, wages
SUMIFS of expenses for the month
What is left after all costs
Net profit as a share of sales

blocks.text: Why not simply sales minus purchases? Because you rarely sell exactly what you bought in the same month. If you stock up heavily, purchases look huge and the month seems to make a loss, even though the goods are still on your shelves. COGS corrects for that by adjusting for the stock you started and finished with.

blocks.title: From sales to net profit
items: Sales
Minus cost of goods
Gross profit
Minus running expenses
Net profit
blocks.caption: Each step removes one layer of cost until only true profit is left.

blocks.text: The report layout

head: Cell
Label
Formula or entry
rows: SUMIFS of stock purchases for the month
SUMIFS by category for the month

blocks.title: Worked example: Funke's October report
blocks.context: For example, Funke's October figures, using her stock value of ₦80,250 from Lesson 4.1. All figures are illustrative.
steps: Sales 412000. Opening stock value 95000. Purchases 310000. Closing stock value 80250.
Expenses: shop rent share 25000, transport 8000, phone data 5000, power 12000. Total 50000.
September net profit in column C was 31000. Change in D14: =B14-C14. Percentage change in E14: =IFERROR(D14/C14,"").
blocks.result: October net profit ₦37,250, up ₦6,250 or about 20.2% on September. Of every ₦100 of sales, about ₦21 is gross profit and about ₦9 is net profit.

blocks.text: Where do opening and closing stock values come from? Closing stock value is your Products tab total (units on the shelf multiplied by cost price) after your monthly count. Next month, that same figure becomes the opening stock value, so the two months link together. If you have not yet built a full inventory, count what is on your shelves on the last day of the month and multiply each item by what you paid for it. An honest estimate is far better than leaving stock out.

blocks.title: Your own drawings are not an expense
blocks.text: Money you take out for yourself or your household is not a business expense. Record it in a separate Drawings category and leave it out of operating expenses. Otherwise the report hides how much the business really earns, and you cannot tell whether it can afford to pay you.
Telling the story in one paragraph

Numbers persuade best with a short explanation. Under the report, write two or three sentences: what happened, why, and what you will do. For example: Net profit rose to ₦37,250 (9% of sales). Sales grew while running costs stayed at ₦50,000. Next month I will reorder detergent earlier because it ran low twice.
Sharing safely

items: **PDF:** Google Sheets: File, Download, PDF. Excel: File, Save As or Export, PDF. A PDF cannot be changed by accident and opens on any phone.
**Protect the formulas:** Excel: Review, Protect Sheet (unlock only input cells first via Format Cells, Protection). Google Sheets: Data, Protect sheets and ranges.
**Share the report, not the tracker:** a lender or partner usually needs the summary and maybe the charts, not every customer's name.
**Keep each month:** duplicate the report tab and name it, for example Report Oct 2026, before changing the dates for the next month.

blocks.title: Check the report against reality
blocks.text: Net profit should roughly match the growth in your cash plus stock, after drawings. If the report says ₦37,250 profit but your money and stock went down, look for unrecorded expenses, unpaid customer debts or drawings recorded as expenses.

takeaways: COGS = opening stock value + purchases - closing stock value.
Gross profit = sales - COGS; net profit = gross profit - running expenses.
Margins divide profit by sales and let you compare months of different sizes.
Keep owner's drawings out of expenses.
Share a protected report or PDF, not your full customer records.

lessons.title: Your complete business workbook: routine, sharing and next steps
objectives: Organise all your tabs into one clear business workbook
Follow a daily, weekly and monthly spreadsheet routine
Share a workbook with the right access level and recover earlier versions
Plan your next spreadsheet skills, such as PivotTables and conditional formatting

blocks.text: You now have the parts of a real business system: a tracker, a summary, charts, an inventory and a profit report. This last lesson puts them together, gives you a routine that keeps the numbers trustworthy, and points to what to learn next.

blocks.name: dashboard
blocks.alt: A person viewing a dashboard of charts and key numbers
blocks.caption: Your finished workbook works like a simple dashboard for your business.

blocks.text: One workbook, clearly organised

head: Tab
Purpose
Built in
rows: Categories, product codes and other drop-down options
Every sale and expense, one row each
Prices, stock levels, reorder alerts, stock value
SUMIF totals by category, product and customer

blocks.text: Give tabs short names, and colour the input tabs (Tracker, Products, Lists) differently from the calculated tabs (Summary, Charts, Report). In Excel right-click a tab and choose Tab Color; in Sheets tap the tab and choose Change colour. Keep a cell at the top of the Summary tab with the date of the last entry, so you can see at once if the records are up to date: =MAX(Tracker!A:A), formatted as a date.

blocks.title: Your spreadsheet routine
items: Daily: record every transaction
Weekly: check and reconcile
Monthly: report and back up
Quarterly: review and decide
blocks.caption: Small, regular habits keep the numbers trustworthy without taking much time.

blocks.text: The routine in detail

items: **Daily (5 to 10 minutes):** enter the day's sales and expenses. Compare the transfer total with your Opay, Moniepoint or bank app and the cash total with the cash in hand.
**Weekly (15 minutes):** run the check cell, compare COUNT and COUNTA, look at the Reorder list, and chase any Unpaid sales.
**Monthly (30 to 45 minutes):** count stock, update the Products tab, produce the profit report, download a backup copy and start a new month.
**Quarterly:** look at three months of charts together and make one decision, such as dropping a slow product or changing a supplier.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's four-week review
blocks.context: For example, at the end of October Bisi looks at the net weekly result (money in minus money out) from her tracker: week 1 84000, week 2 71500, week 3 90000, week 4 66000.
steps: Total in B6: =SUM(B2:B5). Average in B7: =AVERAGE(B2:B5).
Weakest week in B8: =MIN(B2:B5); she filters week 4 in the tracker to see why.
The filter shows two gas refills in week 4 instead of one, and fewer plates sold on a rainy Thursday.
She decides to buy a larger gas cylinder refill and to offer takeaway on WhatsApp on rainy days.
blocks.result: Four-week total ₦311,500, average ₦77,875 a week, weakest week ₦66,000. The spreadsheet did not just store numbers: it pointed her to two specific changes to test in November.

blocks.text: Sharing and access

items: **Google Sheets:** tap Share, add the person's email and choose Viewer (can only look), Commenter (can add comments) or Editor (can change things). Give Editor only to people who really need to type in the sheet.
**Excel:** save to OneDrive, then use Share to send a link and choose whether people can edit or only view.
**Version history** lets you see who changed what and restore an earlier version (Sheets: File, Version history; Excel with OneDrive: File, Info, Version History).

**Moving between programs:** Google Sheets opens .xlsx files and can download as .xlsx; Excel opens downloaded Sheets files. Everything in this course works in both, though some formatting may shift. Check your formulas after converting.

blocks.title: Remove access when people leave
blocks.text: If a staff member or helper stops working with you, remove their access to the file the same day. Also check that no link set to Anyone with the link can edit is floating around WhatsApp groups.
What to learn next

items: **PivotTables** (Excel: Insert, PivotTable; Sheets: Insert, Pivot table) build summary tables by dragging fields, without writing SUMIF formulas.
**Conditional formatting** (Home, Conditional Formatting in Excel; Format, Conditional formatting in Sheets) colours cells automatically, for example Reorder in red.
**Keyboard shortcuts** such as Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+T and Ctrl+Shift+L save time on a computer.
**Formal certification:** Microsoft offers the Microsoft Office Specialist exams in Excel through Certiport test centres if you want a recognised certificate for employment.
**Free practice:** GCFGlobal (LearnFree) has free Excel and Google Sheets lessons, and Microsoft and Google publish help pages for every function used here.

blocks.title: Teach it to someone
blocks.text: Explaining your tracker to a family member or staff member is the fastest way to find gaps in your own understanding, and it means someone can keep records when you are away.

takeaways: Keep all tabs in one workbook, with input tabs and calculated tabs clearly separated.
A daily, weekly, monthly and quarterly routine keeps records accurate.
Share with the lowest access level that works and remove access promptly.
Version history and monthly downloads protect you from mistakes and loss.
PivotTables and conditional formatting are the natural next skills.

quiz.q: A product had opening stock 30, stock in 20 and sold 35. Its reorder level is 12. What do Closing stock and Status show?
quiz.explain: Closing = 30 + 20 - 35 = 15. Since 15 is more than 12, =IF(H2<=I2,"Reorder","OK") shows OK.

quiz.q: Ada's Excel 2016 shows #NAME? for her XLOOKUP formula. What should she do?
options: Use VLOOKUP with FALSE instead, because Excel 2016 does not have XLOOKUP
quiz.explain: XLOOKUP exists only in Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, Excel for the web and Google Sheets. Older versions do not recognise the name.

quiz.q: In =VLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$F$100,4,FALSE), what does the 4 mean?
options: Return the value from the 4th column of the table
quiz.explain: The column number counts from the first column of the table range, so 4 is column D.

quiz.q: Opening stock value 60000, purchases 150000, closing stock value 50000. What is the cost of goods sold?
Sales are 300000, COGS 210000 and operating expenses 45000. What is net profit and net margin?
A helper who updated your Google Sheet has stopped working with you. What should you do?
options: Remove their access in the Share settings the same day
Leave their access in case they return
quiz.explain: Removing access promptly protects your records and your customers' personal data.

finalQuiz.q: Which cell address means column D, row 7?
finalQuiz.explain: Cells are named column letter first, then row number.

finalQuiz.q: Rukayat types her prices as 'N2500'. What problem will this cause?
options: None, the sheet understands the N
The sheet will convert them to dollars
The prices are treated as text, so SUM and multiplication will not use them
finalQuiz.explain: Type numbers only, then use a naira number format for display.

finalQuiz.q: Her daily sales in B2:B6 are 10000, 15000, 5000, 20000 and 10000. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B6) return?
A discount rate sits in H2. Which formula in E2 can be copied down to give each discounted price from D2?
finalQuiz.explain: The price must move row by row; the single rate cell must be locked with $.

finalQuiz.q: What does =IF(G2>50000,"Big","Normal") show when G2 is 50000?
finalQuiz.explain: 50000 is not greater than 50000, so the test is false and IF returns Normal. Use >= to include 50000.

finalQuiz.q: A margin formula shows #DIV/0!. What is happening?
options: A lookup did not find a code
It is dividing by zero or an empty cell
finalQuiz.explain: #DIV/0! always means the divisor is zero or empty.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the safe way to sort your tracker by amount?
options: Click inside the data and use Data, Sort with headers ticked, so whole rows move together
Select only the Amount column and sort
Cut and paste rows by hand
finalQuiz.explain: Sorting the whole range keeps each row's details together.

finalQuiz.q: Categories are in C2:C200 and amounts in G2:G200. Which formula counts how many Transport entries there are?
finalQuiz.explain: COUNTIF counts rows in the category range that match Transport. SUMIF would add their amounts instead.

finalQuiz.q: Ifeoma wants to show what share of her spending goes to each of four categories. Which chart fits best?
options: A chart with the axis starting at 1000
finalQuiz.explain: A pie shows parts of one whole and is readable with a few slices.

finalQuiz.q: Her VLOOKUP returns the wrong product's price. Her formula is =VLOOKUP(B2,Products!$A$2:$D$50,4). What is the most likely fix?
options: Add FALSE as the last argument for an exact match
finalQuiz.explain: Without FALSE, VLOOKUP looks for an approximate match and can return a neighbouring row's value.

finalQuiz.q: Sales 500000, COGS 380000, operating expenses 70000. What is the gross margin?
finalQuiz.explain: Gross profit 500000 - 380000 = 120000. Gross margin 120000 / 500000 = 24%. Net profit would be 50000, a 10% net margin.

finalQuiz.q: A lender asks to see how your business is doing. What is the best thing to share?
options: Editor access to your whole workbook including customer phone numbers
A PDF of your monthly profit report and a sales chart
Your phone with the sheet open
Nothing, because spreadsheets cannot show profit
finalQuiz.explain: Share the summary evidence in a form that cannot be changed, and keep customers' personal data private.
